beats.text: EMG to ankle torque: what the code actually does. We follow experiment D01, the model the dashboard calls Balanced positions, from the raw recordings to every R² on the dashboard.

There are six people, known here only by their codes: CH, EG, HM, IES, JM and YES. Each has one recording file. We follow EG all the way through, and bring in the others where they behave differently.

EG's file holds {eg_n_trials} trials in recording order. First, {eg_n_mvc} maximal contractions of {eg_mvc_s} seconds, which this model never uses. Then session one, which the lab calls test: at each of eight ankle angles, a passive trial followed by an active trial. Then session two, the retest: the same eight angles in the same order.

Every trial stores six channels at 1000 samples per second: four surface EMG signals, from the medial and lateral gastrocnemius, called GM and GL, the soleus, and the tibialis anterior, TA, plus the ankle angle in radians and the torque in Nm.

Here is one active trial: EG at {eg_angle} rad. The dynamometer holds the ankle still; the angle's standard deviation is only {eg_angle_sd} mrad. For {eg_active_s} seconds, EG pushes {eg_pushes} times. Pushing the toes down makes the torque negative.

The eight angles run from {eg_ang_min} rad, toes down, to {eg_ang_max} rad, toes up: negative means plantarflexed. The pushes are small at the toes-down end, reaching about {eg_peak_min} Nm, and about {eg_peak_max} Nm at the toes-up end.

Session one and session two are separate blocks of trials in the same file, recorded on the same day. In between, the electrodes and the tissue can change. The real question is whether a model trained on session one still works on session two.
The task: from the last 0.2 seconds of muscle signals and ankle angle, predict the torque the muscles are producing right now. Train on session one; score on session two, which the model never sees.
Three things make this hard. First, the EMG size changes between sessions. For JM at {jm_angle} rad, the session-two soleus signal per Nm of push is only {jm_sol_before} times its session-one size.

Second, passive torque. Even with relaxed muscles, stretched tissue pulls on the ankle: about {eg_map_low} Nm at EG's most toes-down angle and {eg_map_high} Nm at the toes-up end, and the values differ between sessions. The EMG cannot see any of it.

Third, the toes-down pushes are small. At {sd_min_angle} rad, EG's active torque has a standard deviation of {sd_min} Nm; at {sd_max_angle} rad, {sd_max} Nm. One Nm of error is minor at one end and half the signal at the other, and a plain loss barely notices the small angles.

Here is the whole pipeline for EG. The top branch uses session one only. The raw EMG becomes a smooth envelope, is divided by the session-one maximum, and is auto-gained. A passive map from still holds is subtracted from the measured torque, giving the active-torque target. 0.2-second windows train a small LSTM, with every angle scaled to count the same.

The bottom branch is session two. The same preprocessing runs with session one's settings, the frozen model predicts, and the prediction is scored against session two's own active torque, built from session two's own passive map.

In the code, one job is one call of run experiment: prepare builds the arrays, fit predict trains and predicts. Prepare also detects rest periods and fits a passive model, but with the static passive setting that fit returns at once, so those steps change nothing for D01.
The preprocessing, on one real three-second piece of EG's soleus signal. First, the mean of the whole trial is subtracted: an offset of {env_mean} recorded units.
Then a fourth-order Butterworth band-pass, 30 to 300 hertz, removes drift and movement artefacts below 30 hertz and noise above 300. It runs forward and then backward, so it adds no delay.
Rectification takes the absolute value, so every oscillation becomes a positive bump.

A 2 hertz low-pass, also run forward and backward, smooths that into the envelope: the size of the muscle's activity. Running backward means using the future: 90 % of this filter's weight lies within {imp90} seconds on either side, so the envelope, as coded, could not be computed in real time.

The first second of every trial is dropped. Then the envelope is decimated by ten with an anti-aliasing filter: 1000 samples per second become 100, one value every ten milliseconds. The angle and the torque go through the same decimation.
Each active trial is now {n100} samples long: {sec100} seconds of four envelopes, the angle and the torque.

Scaling has two steps. Step one divides each muscle by its largest envelope value in session one, taken on the one-kilohertz envelope over whole trials, including the parts later used for validation. Session two is divided by the same session-one numbers.

Step two, auto-gain, is switched on only for people who push in one direction. For each session-one trial, the code compares the torque during the top fifth of muscle activity with the torque during the bottom fifth. EG's eight differences are all negative, from {eg_dir_hi} to {eg_dir_lo} Nm, so auto-gain is on. CH pushes both ways, from {ch_dir_hi} to {ch_dir_lo} Nm, so for CH it is off.

Auto-gain rescales each muscle from its own recent past. Every half second the code looks back: the floor is the 10th percentile of the last 20 seconds, the top is the 95th percentile of the last 45 seconds. Only past samples are used, so this step is causal.

Early in a trial there is little past, so each value is blended with a prior from session one's training data. The data's weight is n over n plus 500, where n is the number of past samples, so after 5 seconds data and prior count equally. Because the windows stop growing, the prior never fades completely: it keeps 20 % of the floor and 10 % of the top.

One rescale, worked through, for JM's session-two soleus. At {wx_t} seconds, the floor window holds {wx_n_lo} samples, so the data weight is {wx_w_lo}: the floor is {wx_floor}. The top is {wx_top}, so the range is {wx_range}, above the minimum of 0.35 times the prior range, {wx_rmin}. The value {wx_x} becomes value minus floor, divided by range: {wx_a}. Results are clipped between 0 and 2.
Before that, spikes more than four ranges above the floor are held at the last good value for 0.3 seconds: {eg_despiked} of EG's samples.

For JM at {jm_angle} rad, session two's size per Nm, relative to session one, goes from {jm_gm_before} to {jm_gm_after} for GM, {jm_gl_before} to {jm_gl_after} for GL, and {jm_sol_before} to {jm_sol_after} for the soleus. Over all of EG's angles, the typical mismatch shrinks from {eg_mis_before} times to {eg_mis_after} times.

One more thing only the code shows: auto-gain divides by a range measured on the same signal, so step one's division cancels out, except where the spike detector's fixed threshold of 0.1 applies: {cancel_pct} % of EG's samples, in {cancel_trials} trials.

Now passive torque. Before each active trial comes a passive trial. Its first {hold_s} seconds hold the ankle still at the coming angle, with the torque steady to a few hundredths of a Nm. Then the device steps to another angle and the torque swings by tens of Nm.

The code cuts each passive trial wherever the angle jumps faster than 5 radians per second, skips one second after each jump, and keeps a piece only if it lasts at least 5 seconds, its angle varies by at most 5 mrad, and its torque by at most 1 Nm. Nothing checks the EMG: relaxed means a still piece of a trial labelled passive.

Each piece that passes gives one map point: its mean angle and its mean torque. Points within 0.05 rad are averaged. For EG, {eg_kept} of {eg_pieces} pieces pass: the first {hold_s} seconds of every passive trial, eight points per session. So the map is not an average over every moment at that angle; the active trials contribute nothing. Session two gets its own map from its own holds.

Three exceptions. For YES, the map is a hand-entered table in the config file. IES has no passive trials, so nothing is subtracted and the target is the measured torque. And one of JM's passive trials contains movement, which the stillness test throws out.

The target is measured torque minus the map, read at every sample's angle by straight-line interpolation. For EG at {eg_angle} rad the session-one map gives about {p_s1} Nm. Training targets use the session-one map; the scoring target uses the session-two map, about {p_s2} Nm here.

The model never sees a whole trial. It sees windows: 20 samples in a row, 0.2 seconds, of five inputs: the four scaled envelopes and the ankle angle in radians. The target is the active torque at the window's last sample. Then the window moves on by one sample, ten milliseconds.
{n100} samples give {n_windows} windows per trial.

Session one is split inside every trial. The first 80 % of windows, {n_train}, are for training. The rest are validation, minus the very last window, which the experiment script drops to match the original code: {n_val}.

There is no gap between the parts. The first validation window shares 19 of its 20 input samples with training windows, and the first 19 validation windows all overlap training data. Their targets are new; their inputs are not. Last week's pipeline left a one-second gap and filtered each part separately.
Across EG's eight session-one trials, that makes {x_train} training windows and {x_val} validation windows, each 20 by 5. The test set is every window of all eight session-two trials: {x_test}.

Shuffle equals true means one thing: at the start of every epoch, Keras shuffles the order of the training windows, mixing trials and angles, and cuts them into batches of 8. Validation windows are never trained on; they are only measured, to decide when to slow down and when to stop. Session two plays no part in training. The reverse direction is the same with the sessions swapped, run with three seeds instead of ten.
Now the change behind the name balanced positions. The training angles are grouped into knots; angles closer than 0.02 rad would be merged. EG has eight knots, one per angle.

For each knot, the code takes the standard deviation of the training targets at that angle, with a floor of 0.1 Nm. For EG that runs from {sd_min} Nm at the toes-down end to {sd_max} Nm at {sd_max_angle} rad. The dashboard calls this each angle's swing; in the code it is the standard deviation, from the training part only.
The model trains on each target divided by its angle's standard deviation, and its output is multiplied back by the standard deviation of the nearest knot, which gives Nm again.

Why it matters: for one angle, the sum of squared errors equals the number of windows, times the standard deviation squared, times one minus R². So under plain mean squared error, EG's {sd_max_angle} rad counts {sd2_ratio} times more than {sd_min_angle} rad for the same R². After dividing, every angle has {n_train} windows, and the loss is the sum of one minus R² over the angles: each angle counts the same.

In the trained model the difference is visible: with plain squared errors, the toes-down angle would carry {share_plain_low} % of the training loss; with the scaled loss it carries {share_scaled_low} %.

The model is small. An LSTM layer with eight units that passes on its output at every step, 30 % dropout, a second eight-unit LSTM that passes on only its last output, dropout again, and one linear output: {n_params} numbers in total.

At every step, the input and the layer's previous output are combined into four groups of eight numbers. The input, forget and output gates go through a sigmoid, between 0 and 1; the candidate goes through tanh. The new memory is the old memory times the forget gate, plus the candidate times the input gate. The output is tanh of the memory, times the output gate.

One real window: EG, session two, {eg_angle} rad, as a push begins, through the trained model. At the first step the inputs are these five numbers. For unit {cell_unit} of layer one, the input gate sums to {cell_zi}, which the sigmoid turns into {cell_i}. The forget gate is {cell_f}, the candidate {cell_g}, the output gate {cell_o}. The memory starts at zero, so the new memory is {cell_c}, and the output is {cell_h}.

The same arithmetic repeats 20 times, feeding each output back in. These are layer one's eight outputs and memories across the window. Layer two keeps only its last output, eight numbers, and the dense layer turns them into one: {cell_yhat}. Times this angle's standard deviation, {cell_sd} Nm, that is {cell_pred} Nm; the measured active torque was {cell_true} Nm.

Training starts from the seed. Set random seed seeds Python, NumPy and TensorFlow. Python's generator fixes the starting weights and the two dropout layers' masks; TensorFlow's seed fixes the shuffle. Layer one's input weights start uniform within plus or minus {glorot1}, recurrent weights start orthogonal, and the forget-gate biases start at one.

Step one. The first shuffled batch holds eight windows from {batch_n_angles} different angles. Each target is divided by its angle's standard deviation. With dropout on, the model predicts these eight values, and the loss is the mean of the eight squared differences: {batch_loss}.

Back-propagation gives a gradient for every one of the {n_params} weights. Nadam keeps running means of the gradients and of their squares, corrects both for the first steps, adds a look-ahead on the first, and divides one by the square root of the other. On step one that moves every weight by almost exactly {step1_size}, whatever its gradient. This weight has gradient {nd_g} and moves from {nd_w0} to {nd_w1}.
Here are the first five steps: the batch loss, and three weights moving. One epoch is {n_steps_epoch} such steps.

After each epoch Keras measures the validation loss with dropout off; the training loss it reports is an average over the epoch with dropout on, so the two curves sit at different levels. EG's best validation loss came at epoch {best_epoch}: {best_val}. Ten epochs without an improvement of at least 0.0001 cut the learning rate by 30 %, after epoch {lr_cut1} and again after epoch {lr_cut2}. Twenty-five epochs without any improvement stopped training after epoch {n_epochs}, and the weights from epoch {best_epoch} were put back. Those weights predict session two.
This rerun is the saved run: same epochs, same best validation loss, and test predictions identical to the saved ones, to the last bit.

Prediction is one pass over all {x_test} session-two windows, with dropout off. Each output is multiplied by the standard deviation of the knot nearest to its trial's angle, which turns it back into Nm.
Here is every session-two trial of EG with seed 0: the measured active torque in white, the prediction in green, with each trial's R² and mean absolute error.

The dashboard's numbers come from the presentation metrics script. It compares the prediction with active torque, measured torque minus the tested session's passive map, at every window's last sample. Not total torque. For IES, with no map, that is the measured torque itself.

One angle, computed live: EG, {eg_angle} rad, seed 0, {live_n} samples. Add up the squared errors: the residual sum, {live_ss_res} Nm². Add up the squared distances from this trial's own mean: the total sum, {live_ss_tot} Nm². R² is one minus their ratio: {live_r2}. Zero would mean no better than a flat line at the trial's own mean.
The mean absolute error is {live_mae} Nm. The dashboard shows it next to the peak target, the largest absolute active torque in this trial: {live_peak} Nm. That is a peak torque, not a peak error.
Every angle and every seed fills EG's table: eight angles by ten seeds, eighty values. Any negative R² is set to zero first; then each angle takes the median over its ten seeds.

Across people, each person-and-angle cell gets one vote. The headline R² is the median of all {cells} cell medians: {head_r2}; the mean absolute error the same way: {head_mae} Nm. The toes-down group, each person's two most negative angles, gives {toes_r2}; the other {other_cells} cells give {other_r2}.

In the box plots, the whiskers are the 5th and 95th percentiles over the ten seeds at each angle; with ten seeds, the 5th percentile sits just above the worst seed. On the overview cards the range is taken differently: the median over the cells within each seed, then percentiles across the seeds.

Last week's pipeline, for contrast. It used half-second windows and every fifth training window, cut a one-second gap at the split and filtered each part separately, divided the EMG by its training maximum without auto-gain, and standardised the target once for all angles. It trained in batches of 64, for at most 60 epochs with patience 12. On EG at {eg_angle} rad, seed 0, it scored R² {lw_r2} and a mean absolute error of {lw_mae} Nm, against {live_r2} and {live_mae} Nm for D01.

In one breath: turn the EMG into smooth envelopes, rescale them from their own recent past, subtract a passive map measured in still holds, show a small LSTM 0.2-second windows with every angle weighted equally, and score each person and angle on a session it never saw.
